title: GDPR & Multi-Tenant Architecture
description: A German enterprise client is evaluating your LMS platform. Navigate the architecture interview — from data isolation to tenant routing and cache invalidation.

steps.interviewerSays: A German enterprise client asks: How is their data isolated from other tenants on your platform?
steps.context: Opening question. They want to see if you understand multi-tenancy models at depth — and whether you recognise that GDPR changes the answer.

options.text: Shared database with TenantId column on every table, enforced via row-level security
options.interviewerReaction: Hmm — that handles logical isolation, but what about GDPR data residency requirements for this specific client?

options.text: Dedicated Geo-Pod in Germany with isolated compute, database, cache, storage and logging
options.interviewerReaction: Good thinking. You addressed both isolation and data residency. Now — how do you identify which tenant a request belongs to?

options.text: Separate database per tenant, hosted globally in the nearest region
options.interviewerReaction: You addressed database isolation but missed the data residency requirement — this client's data cannot leave German soil under GDPR Article 46.

idealAnswer.summary: For a GDPR-regulated German client, the correct approach is a full regional Geo-Pod deployment — not just database isolation.

sections.heading: The Three Multi-Tenancy Models
sections.content:
Multi-tenancy has three primary isolation models:

• Pool Model — Shared database with TenantId on every table. Cheapest to operate, but weak isolation and fails GDPR data residency.

• Bridge Model — Shared database server, separate schema per tenant. Better logical isolation, still same physical infrastructure.

• Silo Model — Dedicated database (and optionally compute) per tenant. Strongest isolation. For GDPR clients, Silo is mandatory regardless of their plan tier.

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: GDPR compliance overrides cost optimisation decisions — bill it as a Data Residency Premium tier
ALL layers must be regional: compute, cache, database, blob storage, and logs
Backups replicate only to the paired EU region (Germany North ↔ Germany West Central)
Log Analytics is the layer teams most commonly forget — it contains IP addresses and user activity
The Global Control Plane (auth, billing) can stay centralised — it holds no PII from this tenant

sections.heading: Most Common Production Mistake
sections.content: Teams correctly isolate the SQL database but forget that Redis cache and Log Analytics workspaces also contain PII — user sessions, activity logs, IP addresses. All of these must stay within the German region boundary. A single misconfigured Log Analytics workspace sending data to West Europe will constitute a GDPR breach.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Full GDPR compliance and legal defensibility under Article 46
Strong tenant isolation at every infrastructure layer
Independent backup, restore, and failover per tenant
Pod can be suspended or destroyed independently (tenant offboarding)
cons: Higher infrastructure cost — mitigate by charging as a Data Residency Premium tier
More complex automated onboarding pipeline (Infrastructure-as-Code required)
Operational overhead: managing, monitoring, and patching regional stacks separately

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: GDPR compliance is not just a database decision — it is a full-stack regional architecture decision covering compute, cache, storage, and logs.

steps.interviewerSays: Good. Now walk me through how your platform identifies which tenant a request belongs to, and routes it to the correct regional pod.
steps.context: Tenant identification and routing is where many systems have subtle security bugs. They want to see if you think about spoofing, header injection, and multi-region routing.

options.text: Read TenantId from a custom request header — X-Tenant-Id — set by the client application
options.interviewerReaction: That is a serious security issue — any client can forge that header and access another tenant's data. How would you prevent that?

options.text: Use subdomain-based routing — client.yourdomain.com — extract tenant from the Host header, look up in a tenant registry, then route to the correct pod
options.interviewerReaction: Solid. Subdomain routing is the industry standard. Now tell me — what happens to cached data when a tenant is suspended?

options.text: Embed TenantId in the JWT access token at login time and read it from the token on every request
options.interviewerReaction: JWT claims are a good secondary signal, but the primary routing decision should happen before token validation — at the gateway level. What if the token is stolen and replayed?

idealAnswer.summary: Tenant identification should happen at the network edge using subdomain-based routing — before any application code runs. JWT claims are a secondary validation layer, not the primary routing mechanism.

sections.heading: Tenant Identification Strategies
sections.content:
There are three common patterns for identifying tenants in a multi-tenant API:

1. Custom Header (X-Tenant-Id) — Simple but dangerous. Any caller can forge the header. Never use as sole identification mechanism.

2. JWT Claims — Include tenantId in the token payload. Secure against forgery (token is signed), but routing still needs to happen before the token is decoded.

3. Subdomain Routing — client.yourdomain.com. The Host header is set by the network stack, not by client code. Extract at the API Gateway or reverse proxy layer before requests reach application code.

sections.heading: Request Routing Flow
sections.content:
Browser: acme.yourdomain.com/api/courses
                    │
                    ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Azure Front Door / APIM       │
  │  Extract: host = acme.*         │
  │  Lookup:  TenantRegistry[acme]  │
  │  Route:   → EU Geo-Pod (DE)     │
  │  Inject:  X-Tenant-Id (signed)  │
  └────────────┬────────────────────┘
               │ (internal signed header)
               ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Application Layer (AKS)       │
  │  Validate X-Tenant-Id HMAC      │
  │  Validate JWT tenantId claim    │
  │  Proceed with DB + Cache ops    │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Tenant resolution must happen at the gateway — before application code — to enable correct pod routing
If you must pass tenant context as a header internally, sign it with HMAC so application code can verify it was set by the gateway, not a malicious caller
JWT tenantId claim provides defence-in-depth — validate it matches the gateway-resolved tenant
The tenant registry (id → pod endpoint mapping) must be highly available — a cache miss here blocks all tenants
Use wildcard TLS certificates (*.yourdomain.com) to support unlimited tenant subdomains without certificate provisioning delays

sections.heading: Security Anti-Pattern: Trusting Client-Supplied TenantId
sections.content: Never trust a TenantId that comes directly from the client request body or an unvalidated header. This is a Broken Object Level Authorisation (BOLA) vulnerability — OWASP API Security #1. An attacker can change the TenantId to access another tenant's data. All tenant identification must be resolved server-side from a trusted signal (subdomain, signed token) and validated at every layer.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Subdomain routing enables pod-level routing before any app code runs
HMAC-signed internal headers prevent lateral movement across pods
Dual validation (gateway + JWT) gives defence in depth
cons: Requires wildcard DNS and TLS certificate management
Tenant registry becomes a critical dependency — must be cached aggressively
Adds latency at gateway for registry lookup — mitigate with in-memory cache with short TTL

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Tenant identity must be resolved at the network edge from a trusted signal — subdomain routing — never from client-supplied headers or request bodies.

steps.interviewerSays: Last one. Acme Corp violates their contract — you need to suspend their tenant immediately. Their data is cached in Redis. Walk me through your cache invalidation strategy.
steps.context: This tests operational thinking. Suspension must be instant, complete, and verifiable. Many engineers only think about the database — the cache is where suspended tenants continue to get service.

options.text: Set a suspended flag in the database. On next cache miss, the application will read the flag and block the request.
options.interviewerReaction: What about the existing cached entries? A suspended tenant could continue to receive service for the full TTL of every cached key — potentially hours. How do you close that gap?

options.text: Flush the entire Redis instance to clear all cached data for the suspended tenant.
options.interviewerReaction: That would evict all other tenants' cached data too — you'd cause a cache stampede across your entire platform. You need a targeted approach.

options.text: Use a Redis key namespace per tenant (tenant:{id}:*), issue a SCAN + DELETE pipeline for that namespace, push a suspension event to a pub/sub channel, and update the tenant registry to return 403 at the gateway — all as an atomic suspension workflow.
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right. Immediate gateway block plus targeted cache eviction plus event propagation. That is a production-grade suspension workflow.

idealAnswer.summary: Tenant suspension must be immediate and operate at three layers simultaneously: gateway (stop new requests), cache (evict existing data), and database (persist suspended state). Missing any layer creates a gap window.

sections.heading: The Three-Layer Suspension Model
sections.content:
A correct suspension workflow operates at three layers simultaneously:

1. Gateway Layer — Update the tenant registry to return HTTP 403 for this tenant's subdomain. This stops new requests immediately without touching any backend systems.

2. Cache Layer — Evict all Redis keys for this tenant's namespace using a targeted SCAN + DEL pipeline. This prevents serving cached data to the suspended tenant.

3. Persistence Layer — Mark the tenant as suspended in the database. This provides the authoritative state that survives pod restarts and cache eviction.

sections.heading: Suspension Workflow
sections.content:
Admin triggers: POST /admin/tenants/acme/suspend
                        │
              ┌─────────┴──────────┐
              │  Suspension        │
              │  Orchestrator      │
              └──┬──────┬──────┬───┘
                 │      │      │
        ┌────────┘   ┌──┘   ┌──┘
        ▼            ▼      ▼
  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
  │ Tenant   │ │  Redis   │ │  Database    │
  │ Registry │ │  Evict   │ │  suspended=  │
  │ → 403    │ │ tenant:  │ │  true        │
  │          │ │ acme:*   │ │              │
  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────────┘
        │            │
        └────────────┘
               │
               ▼
     Pub/Sub: tenant.suspended
        (notify all pods)

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Always prefix Redis keys with tenant namespace: tenant:{tenantId}:{resource} — enables targeted eviction without touching other tenants
Use Redis SCAN + DEL pipeline, never KEYS command in production — KEYS blocks the Redis thread for the full scan duration
Pub/Sub event (tenant.suspended) ensures all pods in the Geo-Pod invalidate their local in-memory caches simultaneously
The gateway 403 is the fastest enforcement point — it activates in milliseconds without cache or DB involvement
Log the suspension event with a timestamp to the audit trail — required for GDPR Article 30 records of processing

sections.heading: The Gap Window Anti-Pattern
sections.content: The most dangerous suspension anti-pattern is updating only the database. If you set suspended=true in the DB but leave cached data in Redis, the suspended tenant continues to receive cached API responses for the full TTL of every key — which could be 15 minutes to several hours depending on your cache policy. During an incident or legal dispute, this gap window is both a security failure and a potential GDPR breach.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Gateway block is instantaneous — no cache TTL gap window
Targeted Redis namespace eviction has no collateral impact on other tenants
Pub/Sub propagation ensures all pods sync state simultaneously
Audit trail satisfies GDPR Article 30 records of processing requirements
cons: SCAN + DEL pipeline has cost proportional to the number of cached keys — acceptable for suspension but design key namespaces to bound this
Pub/Sub delivery is at-most-once — pods that are down during the event may miss it; resolve with a startup check against the tenant registry
Orchestrating three systems atomically requires careful error handling — use a saga pattern with compensation actions if any step fails

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Tenant suspension is a three-layer workflow — gateway block, targeted cache eviction, and DB persistence — and missing any one layer creates a gap window that is both a security failure and a GDPR risk.

bands.label: Ready for this SA role
bands.message: Strong architectural thinking across all dimensions. You demonstrated both breadth and depth — GDPR awareness, security thinking at the routing layer, and operational precision under suspension scenarios.

bands.label: Strong but gaps exist
bands.message: Good fundamentals. Deepen your understanding of compliance architecture, gateway-level security patterns, and operational cache management before your next senior interview.

bands.label: Needs deeper preparation
bands.message: Revisit multi-tenancy fundamentals, GDPR architecture requirements, and distributed systems operational patterns. Focus on thinking in layers — network, cache, compute, storage, and logging.

sections.heading: Multi-Tenancy — Explained Simply
sections.content:
Think about Gmail. You have an account. Your friend has an account. Your boss has an account. All three of you are using the exact same application, running on the exact same Google servers. But you have never seen your boss's emails. Your boss has never seen yours. Millions of people. One platform. Complete separation.

That is multi-tenancy. One software system. Multiple customers. Each customer sees only their own world.

The question every architect has to answer is — how do you actually enforce that separation? Because the data is all sitting on the same machine. The same hard drive. The same database. How does the system know that this row belongs to Acme Corp and that row belongs to Globex Corp — and make absolutely sure they never cross?

Pool Model — Every piece of data gets stamped with a customer ID. Every query filters by that ID. One database, all customers inside it, separated only by a label. Cheap and effective for most products. But the isolation lives entirely in your application code. One developer writes one query and forgets the filter — and Acme Corp is reading Globex Corp's data. The wall between customers is made of trust, not concrete.

Bridge Model — Each customer gets their own dedicated schema within the same database server. The database engine now enforces the boundary — your application code cannot accidentally cross it. A stronger wall. But the physical infrastructure — the server, its backups, its logs — still holds every customer's data together under one roof.

Silo Model — Each customer gets their own database, their own servers, their own everything. Nothing is shared. This is the only model that satisfies legal requirements like GDPR, where a German enterprise client's data cannot physically exist outside Germany — on any server, in any shared space, ever. It costs significantly more to run, which is why mature SaaS platforms bill it as a Data Residency Premium tier and charge accordingly.

These three models are not alternatives — they are tiers. The same platform can offer all three simultaneously. Small customers in the Pool Model. Enterprise customers in the Bridge Model. Regulated enterprise customers in the Silo Model. Your architecture tiering and your pricing tiering are the same decision, described in two different languages.

Multi-tenancy is not about technology. It is about trust. Every customer on your platform is trusting you that their competitor — who may also be your customer — will never see their data. The model you choose is how seriously you take that trust.

sections.heading: GDPR — Explained Simply
sections.content:
GDPR is a law. Specifically a European law. And like most laws, it exists because something went wrong.

For decades, technology companies collected personal data — names, emails, locations, browsing habits, medical history — and did whatever they wanted with it. Sold it. Shared it. Lost it in breaches. Users had no idea what was being collected, where it was going, or how to stop it. Then in 2018, the European Union said enough. They passed the General Data Protection Regulation. GDPR.

At its core GDPR answers one question — who owns your personal data? The answer it gives is simple and radical. You do. Not the company that collected it. Not the platform you signed up on. You. And because you own it, you have rights over it.

You have the right to know what data a company holds about you. You have the right to ask them to delete it. You have the right to know if it has been breached. You have the right to move it to another company. And companies have to ask your permission before collecting it in the first place — real permission, not a 47-page terms and conditions document buried in small print.

For engineers, GDPR translates into one rule above everything else. Personal data of European citizens must stay in Europe. Not on a server in the United States. Not in a data centre in Singapore. Europe. This is called data residency and it is why architecture decisions that seem purely technical are actually legal decisions in disguise.

Here is where most engineering teams make their mistake. They think data residency means the database stays in Europe. So they put the database in a Frankfurt data centre and consider the job done. But GDPR does not care only about the database. It cares about every layer that touches personal data. Your application servers. Your cache. Your file storage. Your logs. Yes — your logs. Because logs contain IP addresses, user identifiers, and activity records. That is personal data. A database in Frankfurt with logs shipping to a data centre in Virginia is a GDPR violation.

The penalty for getting this wrong is not a warning letter. It is a fine of up to twenty million euros or four percent of your global annual revenue — whichever is higher. For a large company that number can be in the billions.

This is why when a German enterprise client asks how their data is isolated on your platform, the answer cannot be a TenantId column in a shared database. The answer has to be a completely dedicated infrastructure stack — compute, database, cache, storage, and logging — all physically located within Germany. The architecture is not a technical preference. It is a legal requirement with a price tag attached to getting it wrong.

GDPR turned data from a technical problem into a legal one. And that changed everything about how serious software is architected.

sections.heading: Redis - Explained Simply
sections.content:
Every application has the same problem. The database is slow. Not broken, not misconfigured — just slow. Because databases are built for permanence. They write data to disk, they maintain indexes, they enforce constraints, they guarantee that nothing is ever lost. All of that reliability comes at a cost. Speed.

Now imagine your application gets a thousand requests every second. Each request asks the same question — who is this user, what are their permissions, what is their account status. A thousand database queries every second for information that has not changed since yesterday. The database is doing enormous work to answer questions it has already answered a thousand times before.

Redis solves this. Redis is a store that lives entirely in memory — not on disk, in RAM. And RAM is orders of magnitude faster than disk. A database query that takes fifty milliseconds takes less than one millisecond in Redis. That difference, multiplied across thousands of requests, is what separates a fast application from a slow one.

The way it works is simple. The first time your application needs a piece of data it goes to the database, gets the answer, and stores a copy in Redis. Every subsequent request for the same data skips the database entirely and reads from Redis instead. This is called a cache. Redis is the most widely used cache in the world.

But Redis is not just a cache. It is a data structure store. It understands lists, sets, sorted sets, and hash maps natively. This makes it useful for things a simple cache cannot do — counting how many times a user has logged in this hour, maintaining a leaderboard that updates in real time, storing a user session with dozens of attributes, or broadcasting a message to thousands of connected clients simultaneously.

The one thing Redis trades away for all this speed is permanence. Because data lives in memory, a server restart means that data is gone. This is why Redis is never your primary database — it is always a layer in front of your real database. The database holds the truth. Redis holds a fast copy of the truth that is good enough for right now.

In a multi-tenant system Redis becomes even more critical. Instead of hitting the database on every request to figure out which tenant this subdomain belongs to, which region their data lives in, and whether their account is active — you cache all of that in Redis. A lookup that would cost fifty milliseconds and a database round trip costs less than a millisecond and never touches the database at all. At scale, that is the difference between an infrastructure bill that is manageable and one that is not.

sections.heading: JWT tokens - Explained Simply
sections.content:
Think about a boarding pass at an airport. You arrive at the check-in counter, show your passport, prove who you are. The airline verifies your identity once — and then hands you a boarding pass. From that moment, nobody asks for your passport again. Every gate you walk through, every lounge you enter, every time someone needs to know who you are — you just show the boarding pass. It has your name, your seat, your flight, your boarding group. Everything needed, right there in your hand. The gate agent does not call the airline database to verify you exist. They just scan the pass.

JWT works exactly like this. You log in with your username and password. The server verifies your credentials once — checks the database, confirms you exist, confirms your password is correct — and then hands you a token. From that moment, the database is out of the picture entirely. Every request you make includes that token. The server reads it, sees your user ID, your role, your permissions — and that is enough. No database call. No lookup. No waiting. The token itself is the proof. One database hit at login. Zero database hits for everything after. In an application handling a million requests a day, that difference is not a minor optimisation — it is what keeps the database alive.

The obvious question is — what stops you from editing that token? Writing yourself a business class seat you did not pay for? This is where the clever part comes in. The airline prints a barcode on your boarding pass that is mathematically tied to everything on it. Change your seat number, the barcode scan fails. The gate agent knows instantly it has been tampered with.

JWT does the same thing. When the server creates your token it signs it with a secret key that only the server knows. That signature is tied to every single piece of information inside the token. Change your user ID, change your role, change anything — the signature immediately becomes invalid. The server checks the signature on every single request. A tampered token is rejected before it gets anywhere near your data.

Now here is the one weakness of this system. Because the server never stores your token — it just hands it to you and forgets it — the server cannot cancel a specific token if something goes wrong. If your account is suspended, if your role changes, if someone steals your token — the server has no way to reach into your pocket and tear up the boarding pass. The only defence is an expiry time. A token that expires in fifteen minutes stops working in fifteen minutes regardless of what happens. Short lived tokens limit the damage. This is the trade-off JWT makes — no database lookups on every request, but no instant revocation either.

JWT did not become the standard because it is perfect. It became the standard because modern applications run across dozens of servers and services simultaneously. A session database that every server has to call on every request becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure at scale. A JWT carries its own proof of identity. Every server, every service, every region can independently verify who you are in microseconds — with nothing but the secret key and the token itself.
